analysis.one_liner: Penalizes companies that move call center jobs overseas and requires agents to disclose their location to callers.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill with 137 cosponsors to penalize companies that offshore call center work never got a committee vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require companies to notify the Labor Department before moving a call center overseas, put those companies on a public list, and make them ineligible for federal grants and guaranteed loans for five years. It would require federal contractors to keep call center work inside the United States, and require customer service agents to tell callers where they are physically located, with the Federal Trade Commission enforcing that disclosure. The bill was introduced by a Republican and drew 137 cosponsors from both parties, but it was sent to four House committees and none of them ever acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Call center workers in the United States, who would get a warning period and a public record before their jobs are moved overseas, and consumers, who would be told where the person answering their call is located and could ask to be transferred to a U.S.-based agent.
analysis.who_benefits_short: U.S. call center workers and consumers

how_it_helps.text: Companies must notify the Labor Department at least 120 days before relocating a call center overseas or contracting that work abroad, and face civil penalties up to $10,000 per day for failing to notify; the Department maintains a public list of companies that do it.

Companies on the list become ineligible for direct or indirect federal grants and federal guaranteed loans for five years, with narrow waivers for national security, U.S. job loss, or environmental harm.

Agencies must require as a condition of federal contracts, civilian and defense-related, that any call center work under the contract be performed inside the United States, and must give contracting preference to employers not on the list.

Customer service agents must disclose their physical location at the start of each call, and a business must transfer a customer who asks to an agent physically located in the United States; the FTC enforces violations as unfair or deceptive practices.
The bill expressly protects workers' federal unemployment, disability, and retraining benefits, so the disclosure and penalties cannot be used to cut off aid to workers whose jobs were moved.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that move or contract out call center work overseas, which would face public listing, loss of federal grants and guaranteed loans for five years, exclusion from federal call center contracts, and compliance costs for location disclosure and transfer requests.
analysis.who_pays_short: Companies that offshore customer service work

drawbacks.text: The bill covers only call centers, a narrow slice of offshored work, so companies could keep moving other back-office jobs abroad; it targets one visible symptom of offshoring rather than the practice generally.

Compliance costs fall on many ordinary businesses, not just offshorers: any business whose agents are partly overseas must verify and disclose locations on every customer contact and certify compliance to the FTC annually, and the $10,000-per-day penalty for a missed 120-day notice is steep for an employer with a large call center.

Requiring call center work on federal contracts to be performed in the United States raises the government's own service costs, since offshore labor is cheaper, a cost that ultimately comes from federal budgets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to workers and consumers are real but modest: notice before layoffs, a public record, and honest disclosure of who is on the phone. The costs are compliance burdens on businesses and somewhat higher federal contract costs. The bill is a targeted disclosure-and-consequence approach rather than an offshoring ban, which limits both its upside and its downside; its main flaw is that it addresses only call centers and leaves the broader offshoring of service work untouched.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees and a consumer protection subcommittee, none of which ever held a markup or sent it to the floor, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Representative David McKinley, a Republican from West Virginia, introduced the bill with Representative Mark Pocan, a Democrat, on June 12, 2019.
The same day, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and, in addition, to the Education and Labor, Armed Services, and Oversight and Reform Committees.
The next day it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce, and no further action was ever taken on the bill.
The bill drew 137 cosponsors: 130 of the 231 House Democrats and 7 of the 197 House Republicans, but that support never produced a committee vote or floor action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that move call center work overseas are better off: no public list, no five-year ban on federal grants and loans, no federal contract requirement, and no location disclosure. The bill never got a vote despite majority-scale cosponsorship, so no one had to go on record against it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies that keep call centers overseas

for.what_they_did: Joined the Republican sponsor in introducing the bill at its introduction.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it majority-caucus support.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill alongside the Republican sponsor.

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill in any of the four committees; it went to a subcommittee and stayed there until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan but lopsided: 130 of 231 Democrats signed on versus 7 of 197 Republicans, with the Republican sponsor supplying the bill's only real GOP support.

industries.industry: Offshore call center and business process outsourcing firms
industries.note: The bill's disclosure and penalty rules attack the core of the offshoring model: cheaper labor abroad answering American customers' calls. U.S. call center jobs and caller transparency come directly at the model's expense.

industries.industry: U.S. companies with overseas customer service operations (banks, telecoms, retailers, tech support)
industries.note: These firms would face annual FTC compliance certification, mandatory location disclosure on every customer contact, and transfer requests to U.S.-based agents, raising the cost of the offshore staffing they use to cut service costs. Their savings come out of service transparency for callers.

industries.industry: Federal contractors performing call center work
industries.note: The bill conditions federal contracts on keeping call center work in the United States and gives preference to employers not on the relocation list, removing the offshore labor cost advantage on government business.

industries.industry: U.S. call center operations and workers
industries.note: Domestic call centers gain a 120-day notice requirement, a public offender list, and contracting preference, making offshoring costlier relative to keeping the jobs in the United States.
